## Research brief — `javax.crypto.Cipher` / `ChaCha20-Poly1305`

### 1. What `Cipher` governs, and what the finding refers to

`javax.crypto.Cipher` is the JCE API class for cryptographic cipher operations—encryption and decryption—and also supports key wrapping and unwrapping. A `Cipher` is created through `Cipher.getInstance`, whose `transformation` argument names the requested algorithm and, where applicable, mode and padding. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/Cipher.html))

For the reported text, the relevant documented API value is the **transformation string supplied to `Cipher.getInstance`**—here, `ChaCha20-Poly1305`. The Java standard-names specification identifies `ChaCha20-Poly1305` as ChaCha20 in AEAD mode using Poly1305; Java SE 25 documentation also lists it among the `Cipher` transformations that every Java platform implementation must support. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html))

The supplied CrySL rule is narrower than that JCA contract: its transformation conditions allow AES, RSA, and listed PBE-with-AES names in the pertinent cases, but do **not** list `ChaCha20-Poly1305`. Thus, the rule source establishes a rule-policy mismatch with that transformation; it does **not** establish that the transformation is invalid under the official `Cipher` API. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/Cipher.crysl))

The string `CipherTransformationUtil` from the detector message does not appear in the provided `Cipher.crysl` source. Its precise implementation and the analyzer’s mapping from that utility to the CrySL constraints cannot be determined from the supplied rule alone.

### 2. Officially documented safe API usage and documented remediation

The official `Cipher` documentation gives these relevant requirements:

- Request a supported transformation with `Cipher.getInstance`. For transformations where mode and padding are relevant, Oracle recommends fully specifying algorithm, mode, and padding rather than relying on provider defaults, because defaults can vary by provider. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/Cipher.html))
- Initialize the object for the selected operation—encryption, decryption, wrapping, or unwrapping—before `update` or `doFinal`. `Cipher` exposes `init` overloads accepting a key and, where required, algorithm parameters and/or a randomness source. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/Cipher.html))
- If an encryption initialization generates required parameters, the API documents obtaining them through `getParameters()` or `getIV()`. Conversely, if required parameters are unavailable during decryption or unwrapping, initialization is documented to fail rather than silently invent parameters. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/Cipher.html))
- For AEAD use, the API documents that AAD must be supplied before ciphertext processing. It also documents that AEAD finalization appends the authentication tag in encryption and verifies it in decryption. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/Cipher.html))
- Specifically for ChaCha20 and ChaCha20-Poly1305, the Javadoc requires unique nonces for a given key and says callers should re-initialize after **each encryption or decryption operation** with parameters specifying a different nonce. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/11/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/Cipher.html))
- Although `doFinal` normally resets a `Cipher` to its post-`init` state, that general reset behavior does not supersede the ChaCha20/ChaCha20-Poly1305 requirement to re-initialize with a different nonce for each operation. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/Cipher.html))

**Documented remediation:** the official `Cipher` sources do not define a remediation that says to replace `ChaCha20-Poly1305` with AES or another transformation merely because an external rule rejects it. In fact, the Java SE documentation recognizes `ChaCha20-Poly1305` as a standard transformation. The documented corrective actions are API-semantic: use a supported explicit transformation, initialize it with appropriate key and parameters, retain/recover needed parameters for decryption, process AAD in the documented order, and avoid nonce reuse for ChaCha20-Poly1305. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/Cipher.html))

### 3. Compatibility, formats, versions, and migration

**Persisted and wire formats.** `Cipher` does not specify a universal serialized ciphertext format or a wire-format migration mechanism. The API does document that cipher parameters can be generated during encryption and retrieved with `getParameters()` or `getIV()`, while decryption without necessary parameters fails. It also documents that AEAD processing includes an authentication tag. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/Cipher.html))

Accordingly, it is an API-based inference—not an Oracle-prescribed format—that data intended for later decryption must make the requisite transformation context and parameters available to the decrypting side, along with any AAD convention required by the application. The JCA API does not prescribe how these items are encoded, versioned, or negotiated. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/Cipher.html))

**Changing the transformation.** The official documentation provides no generic “migration path” that makes ciphertext from one transformation decryptable under another. It documents different transformations, parameters, and AEAD tagging semantics, but no automatic conversion of stored ciphertext, key material, or protocol records between them. This remains an unresolved application-format question in the absence of information about the relevant persistence or protocol specification. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/Cipher.html))

**Platform/version support.**

- The retrieved Java SE 11 Standard Algorithm Names document already lists `ChaCha20-Poly1305` and identifies it as an AEAD construction. The Java 11 API also includes `ChaCha20ParameterSpec`, marked “Since: 11,” for the base ChaCha20 cipher. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/11/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html))
- Java SE 25 `Cipher` documentation explicitly says every Java platform implementation must support the `ChaCha20-Poly1305` transformation. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/Cipher.html))
- Provider support is still an implementation concern for a particular runtime: the standard-names specification states that implementations may support additional algorithms and should document support in release/provider documentation. Oracle’s provider documentation advises general-purpose applications not to pin a provider unless necessary, because that reduces portability. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html))

The supplied sources do not identify the project’s Java runtime baseline, installed providers, or whether another implementation must interoperate. Those are unresolved compatibility facts.

### 4. Exact scope and matching information in `Cipher.crysl`

**Primary rule source:**  
`https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/Cipher.crysl`

The rule’s declared governed type is exactly:

```text
SPEC javax.crypto.Cipher
```

Its factory-event matching clause is exactly:

```text
g1: getInstance(transformation);
g2: getInstance(transformation, _);
Get := g1 | g2;
```

([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/Cipher.crysl))

**Receiver type.** The source declares the specification as `javax.crypto.Cipher`; it does not declare any alternative receiver type. The individual event lines do not add a separate receiver expression. Therefore, **as stated by this rule source, it does not match a method merely because it shares a method name** such as `getInstance`, `init`, `update`, or `doFinal`; its declared API scope is `javax.crypto.Cipher`. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/Cipher.crysl))

**Method names modeled by the rule.** The `EVENTS` block models these names:

- `getInstance`
- `init`
- `update`
- `updateAAD`
- `doFinal`
- `wrap`

It does not define an `unwrap` event. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/Cipher.crysl))

**Parameter-list constraints.** Yes. The source constrains modeled method forms by argument count and by the declared CrySL object variables:

- `getInstance` is modeled as either one `transformation` argument or `transformation` plus a second wildcard argument.
- `init` is modeled in eight forms involving `encmode` plus a certificate or key, optionally with `AlgorithmParameterSpec`, `AlgorithmParameters`, and/or `SecureRandom`.
- `update`, `updateAAD`, and `doFinal` are modeled only for the listed byte-array and `ByteBuffer` forms.
- `wrap` is modeled only as `wrappedKeyBytes = wrap(wrappedKey)`. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/Cipher.crysl))

**Condition evaluated after the transformation is captured.** The source evaluates constraints over `alg(transformation)`, `mode(transformation)`, and `pad(transformation)`, along with initialization mode, input ranges, and named predicates. Relevant transformation restrictions include:

- public/private-key or certificate cases, and wrap/unwrap modes, imply `RSA`;
- a `javax.crypto.SecretKey` implies one of the listed AES or PBE-with-AES algorithm names;
- AES is restricted to GCM, CTR, CTS, CFB, or OFB with `NoPadding`;
- RSA is restricted to the listed mode/padding combinations;
- named requirements cover generated keys, parameters, random sources, IV/GCM/OAEP preparation, and ciphertext/plaintext predicates. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/Cipher.crysl))

Since `ChaCha20-Poly1305` is absent from those transformation allow-lists, the rule source itself explains why it is outside that rule’s admitted set. The source does not call ChaCha20-Poly1305 invalid in the Java Cryptography Architecture; that conclusion would contradict the separate Java standard-name and `Cipher` documentation cited above. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/Cipher.crysl))

### Source limitations

- The CrySL URL is a mutable `refs/heads/master` URL. This research did not independently verify that its fetched content corresponds byte-for-byte to the supplied SHA-256 value or to the detector’s compiled rule artifact.
- The rule file does not document the analyzer’s `CipherTransformationUtil`, its type-resolution behavior, its error-category mapping, or its handling of incomplete programs.
- No project-specific persisted-data format, wire protocol, provider list, Java baseline, key source, nonce lifecycle, or AAD convention was supplied. The official sources therefore do not support a specific migration determination.
